solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 18ac.) Vlog's fiction? Unfortunately, it's become a real threat to many people's material wellbeing

definitions.text: a real threat to many people's material wellbeing

indicators.note: something that goes unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: all twelve letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A lament that made-up video blogging has turned into a danger to people's finances.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue spans two grid entries: 1 across holds COST and 18 across holds OF LIVING. The question mark after 'fiction' hides that it is just raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rising everyday prices for food, fuel and rent erode household budgets, which is exactly the crisis this phrase names.

clue.text: Nick the whip starts to chase Hunt

indicators.note: starts are openings, so only the opening letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the cat o' nine tails is a whip
the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A political picture: the party whip goes after a Tory called Hunt and nicks him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The whip' sounds like a parliamentary enforcer, but it is the cat o' nine tails.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick someone is British slang for arresting them, and arresting a suspect means seizing or capturing them.

clue.text: Attraction of Congress request

blocks.note: congress in the sense of sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: It reads like the pull of a petition made to the US Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks like the American legislature, but here it has its older sense of sexual union.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical allure that draws people toward someone is a kind of attraction, specifically the erotic sort.

clue.text: King George, say – different when topless, matey

indicators.note: topless means with the top removed, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: Georgius Rex, the royal cipher of King George
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does

explanation.surface: Someone describes a king as friendly, and as unlike himself when bare-chested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like it introduces an example of a king, but it is itself EG. GR is the cipher on British postboxes for King George.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone matey is friendly and sociable, and a sociable person who enjoys company is described as gregarious.

clue.text: Talk of ex-deputy PM losing a scrap

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so one letter is dropped

blocks.note: Dominic Raab, a former UK deputy prime minister
taken as written; this is the letter lost

explanation.surface: Gossip about a former deputy prime minister shedding a fight or a fragment.
explanation.walkthrough: RAAB without one A leaves RAB, which then takes BIT. 'Scrap' tempts as a fight, but here it is a small piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, to rabbit (on) is to chatter at length, so it serves as a verb or noun for talk.

clue.text: I say procure the extremes of really ingenious devices

indicators.note: extremes are the two far ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: Gad! is an old exclamation like 'I say!'

explanation.surface: A gadget fan urges someone to buy the most extreme of truly clever contraptions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I say' reads as an instruction, but it is the mild oath Gad.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadgetry is a collective noun for clever mechanical or electronic contrivances, matching a plural description of inventive tools.

clue.text: Told about defunct Democrats' leader

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: Someone was informed about the Democrats' leader who has passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Democrats' leader' pretends to be a person, but it is just the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate a story is to recount or narrate it, so something related has been told to listeners.

clue.text: Pissed more with right Guernsey oyster?

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A drunk asks for more, with the right Channel Island shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English 'pissed' means drunk rather than angry. Guernsey is one of the Channel Islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The ormer is an abalone, an edible shellfish prized in the Channel Islands; calling it an oyster is loose but fair for a delicacy.

clue.text: Mustard spread over todger's tip, good cognitive enhancer

indicators.note: a spread substance is smeared around, so the letters are rearranged
a tip is an extreme end, here the final letter

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of mustard smeared on a penis, sold as a brain booster.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the mixed mustard above the R. Todger is British slang for penis; the tip is its end letter, not its first.
explanation.definitionFit: A nootropic pill taken to boost memory or concentration is popularly called by this name, a drug that makes you clever.

clue.text: A US state spies for Bush?

explanation.surface: American spies at work for President Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' wants to be the president, and the question mark admits the pun: it is a shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: Acacias include many thorny shrubs and small trees, such as wattles, so a bush is a fair example.

clue.text: Hackneyed opinions forced on its rear occupant?

definitions.text: Hackneyed opinions forced on its rear occupant?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a Hackney carriage whose driver lectures the passenger in the back seat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hackneyed' seems to mean clichéd, but a Hackney carriage is the official London name for a licensed cab, and cabbies are famed for sharing their views with the passenger behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hackney carriage is the formal term for a London licensed taxi, whose back-seat rider is its occupant.

clue.text: Cap reversed – a novel predicament

indicators.note: turned back to front, so the letters read the other way

explanation.surface: Wearing your cap backwards creates a new kind of problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A novel' reads as 'a new', but it means a particular book.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a difficult situation with no good choice, a plight or tricky fix.

clue.text: Awful pity heroic Cyclops abandoned two-faced type

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind, so a letter is removed
awful means dreadful, a mess, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the setter, Cyclops, refers to himself as I; this is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: The setter laments having deserted someone heroic, while pointing at a deceiver.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for I, the setter speaking; take one I out of the ten letters before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypocrite professes one set of values while acting on another, showing two faces to the world.

clue.text: Card sticks a Republican in drink

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
a tot is a small drink

explanation.surface: A joker puts a Republican in his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' looks like a funny person, but it is a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarot refers to a card from the pack used in fortune-telling, so one such card is a tarot.

clue.text: Assassin's first approach room?

blocks.note: the first name of Lee Harvey Oswald, who shot President Kennedy
a way or method is an approach

explanation.surface: A killer's first move is to scope the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it means first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway means margin or freedom to manoeuvre, as in having room for error.

clue.text: Buck up king found underneath throne with tart

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing underneath another comes after it

blocks.note: the throne is jokey slang for the toilet
K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: A king is discovered beneath his throne with a prostitute and told to pull himself together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throne' seems royal alongside 'king', but it is the lavatory; 'tart' seems to be a woman, but it is a flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are brisk commands to hurry up and get moving.

clue.text: One who makes expert on crude mad

indicators.note: something mad is deranged, so its letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A maker is an authority on crude madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crude' and 'mad' read as a pair of adjectives, but 'mad' works on 'crude' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A producer manufactures or generates goods, the person or firm behind their creation.

clue.text: Consul besotted with oil, leading to intrigue

indicators.note: a besotted person is intoxicated or infatuated, not in their right order

explanation.surface: A diplomat obsessed with oil money becomes caught up in plots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Besotted with' reads as 'in love with', but it acts on both words together.
explanation.definitionFit: Collusion is a secret agreement to deceive, the kind of scheming plot that intrigue also names.

clue.text: Question about where you can stick speech?

indicators.note: about means around, turned round, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks, rudely, where they can shove a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude 'stick it' tone hides a punctuation answer; 'Question about' looks like 'a query concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Direct speech is written between inverted commas, so that is where spoken words are placed on the page.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Wind up beginning with er, topsy-turvy enterprise

indicators.note: a beginning is the start of something, so only the opening letter is kept
topsy-turvy means upside down, and in a down entry that turns the letters back

blocks.note: to vent is to let out air or wind

explanation.surface: A hesitant 'er' starts the winding-up of a chaotic business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' reads as a phrasal verb for closing a company, but the words split: 'up beginning' gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A venture is a risky business undertaking, the same sense as a commercial enterprise.

clue.text: Camp sailor at first thanks old convict

indicators.note: at first means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
an old lag is a hardened ex-prisoner

explanation.surface: A flamboyant sailor initially gives thanks to a former prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' looks like an adjective for the sailor, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp in the Second World War.

clue.text: In that place that's rid of earth hazard

indicators.note: to be rid of something is to be free of it, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: an old word meaning at that place, there
E is the abbreviation for earth

explanation.surface: A spot that has been cleared of soil is hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: THEREAT is an archaic adverb; remove its first E.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat is a source of possible harm, a danger or menace, which is what a hazard is.

clue.text: "Sexual athlete over the moon!" – film company

indicators.note: in a down entry, over means placed above, so the first piece comes first

blocks.note: a stud is a sexually prolific man
Io is a moon of Jupiter

explanation.surface: A headline about a delighted lothario, attributed to a movie company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the moon' reads as 'delighted', but 'over' positions the pieces and 'the moon' is a named satellite.
explanation.definitionFit: Film studios such as Paramount are production companies, named after the buildings where movies are shot.

clue.text: Establishment also engineered Corbyn's end

indicators.note: engineered means contrived or rebuilt, so the letters are reassembled
an end is the final part, so only the last letter is kept

explanation.surface: The political Establishment also engineered the downfall of Jeremy Corbyn, former Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Establishment' looks like the ruling class, but it means a business premises.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon is a business premises such as a hairdresser's, and an establishment is a place of business.

clue.text: Oh, out of alcohol – terrible for a boozer!

indicators.note: taking something out of a thing removes it
terrible means dreadful or a wreck, so the remaining letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A drinker's cry on discovering the drink has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: A boozer is British slang for a pub, and your local is the pub nearest home.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain your regular neighbourhood pub is called your local, and boozer is slang for a pub.

clue.text: Say collapse leads to complete bankruptcy

explanation.surface: A warning that a business collapse ends in total insolvency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' seems to introduce an example, but it is a verb for speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Total financial ruin is the loss of everything, which is what going completely bankrupt means.

clue.text: In bed but failing to get hard

blocks.note: first meaning: not yet risen in the morning

explanation.surface: A bedroom disappointment of impotence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one embarrassing scene, but each half separately describes the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone still lying down has not risen yet, and a man unable to manage an erection is also lacking one.

clue.text: Bill puts a Conservative on list

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
to list items is to count or enumerate them

explanation.surface: A man called Bill adds a Tory to a list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an invoice.
explanation.definitionFit: An account is a statement of money owed, the same as an invoice or bill presented for payment.

clue.text: Saudi aristocratic holding John Major, Private Eye style

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the letters are held within the words

blocks.note: straddles the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A Saudi nobleman keeps a former British prime minister captive.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye, the British satirical magazine this puzzle comes from, ran the spoof 'Secret Diary of John Major'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the magazine's parody Major wrote a daily journal, so there he is portrayed as someone keeping a diary.

clue.text: Bribe-takers associated with Blair – not finished as a PM!

indicators.note: something not finished lacks its ending, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: to palm money is to take it, so palmers pocket bribes

explanation.surface: Corrupt figures around Tony Blair, whose premiership was cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' leads to his first name, cut short by one letter. Lord Palmerston was a Victorian prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Palmerston served twice as British Prime Minister in the mid-nineteenth century, so he is one example.

clue.text: Excellent deal for a vasectomy?

blocks.note: first meaning: a bargain, in British slang
second meaning: the informal name for the operation

explanation.surface: An advert offering cut-price vasectomies.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a bargain is 'a snip', and the male sterilisation operation is 'the snip'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap bargain is colloquially a steal, and the surgical cutting of the vas deferens is jokingly called by the same word.
